newsitem.title: FRANCE: Peace in Zaire is problem, not Mobutu exit - France. [corrected 21:30 gmt]
newsitem.headline: Peace in Zaire is problem, not Mobutu exit - France. [corrected 21:30 gmt]

text.p: France said on Wednesday the key problem in Zaire was resolving the crisis peacefully rather than arranging the exit of beleagured President Mobutu Sese Seko.

"The problem is not President Mobutu's departure. It's finding a solution to the current crisis. It's aiding the thousands of individuals who are suffering in eastern Zaire," Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said.
Mobutu, battling prostate cancer and rebel advances on the Zairean capital Kinshasa, flew to Gabon's capital Libreville on Wednesay in a visit that triggered speculation he had left Zaire for good.

Rummelhardt told reporters at a regular ministry briefing that international diplomatic efforts under way were "all going in the same direction: finding a peaceful solution for Zaire as quickly as possible".

The spokesman said United Nations special envoy Mohamed Sahnoun was in Paris on Tuesday, briefing French President Jacques Chirac on Sunday's meeting between Mobutu and rebel leader Laurent Kabila and on other initiatves being pursued by Sahnoun and South African President Nelson Mandela.

Chirac telephoned Mandela on Wednesday morning to reiterate France's full support for their efforts for peace and for an orderly transition of power leading to free and open elections in Zaire, the ministry spokesman said.

Washington's United Nations envoy Bill Richardson was expected in Paris on Wednesday evening for additional talks on the Zaire crisis on Thursday with officials at the president's office and the Foreign Ministry, Rummelhardt said. (Corrects to show that meetings will be with presidential and Foreign Ministry aides rather than with the president and foreign minister themselves.)
The flood of pronouncements on Zaire appeared to be an attempt by Paris to show that it was not excluded from the search for an end to the crisis.

French officials had grumbled in recent days that Washington was muscling Paris out of the negotiating process, leaving it on the diplomatic sidelines due to its stubborn support for Mobutu and persistent efforts to block a rebel victory.

Rebel leader Kabila, in an interview with Radio France Internationale, expressed regret about France's position and said his forces intended to form a transitional government regardless of international pressures.
He said he had had contacts with important French officials and said he hoped France's position would change.

"One must obviously take into consideration that we have taken three-quarters of the country, and that we are truly democratic, despite what people try to tell the mass media to discredit the alliance and myself," Kabila said.
"France needs this country, which is one of the largest Francophone countries," he said in the interview, which was conducted in French.

He also rejected UN criticism that the rebels were obstructing attempts to aid Rwandan Hutu refugees stranded in eastern Zaire, saying the charges were "purely a political accusation to try to save a crumbling regime in Zaire".

Kabila's reference to contacts with important French officials may have been a reference to retired French General Jeannou Lacaze, former chief of staff of French armed forces from 1981 to 1985 and Defence Ministry adviser on African affairs from 1985 to 1989, who arrived at rebel headquarters in Lubumbashi on Wednesday.
The French Foreign Ministry confirmed Lacaze's presence but said he was on a private visit and unaccompanied by any French diplomat.

Lacaze, who unsuccessfully tried to launch himself as a major political figure when he left government service, has been best known in recent years as a "point man" for French industries trying to resume ties with embargo-hit Iraq.
